title: Do people keep right in a two-way corridor, and which robot passing policy keeps their lanes?
lede: research programme: do people keep right in a two-way corridor, and what do robots do to their lanes? In two Jülich experiments people with no exit instruction walked on their own right 92 to 94% of the time (HERMES 2009, BaSiGo 2013), and an exit instruction cut that to 0.53 and 0.69; when BaSiGo added information on screens, 99.5% kept right despite the exit instruction; on real city pavements head-on passers kept right only 65% of the time in Zurich and 68% in Nicosia; a social-force crowd twin (JuPedSim) fitted to the free-choice runs kept 0.78 on their right under assigned exits where people kept 0.54, so it over-trusts the convention; moving the exits to the walls only lowers that to 0.68, and a second model family, JuPedSim's anticipation velocity model, keeps 0.996 on their right; a bias that switches off when a walker's exit is on its left, with nothing refitted, brings social force to 0.61 and a third family, the collision-free speed model, to 0.62, while the anticipation model stays at 0.88; a fourth family from another code base, the anticipatory power law, keeps 0.97 with the bias always on and 0.70 with the yielding bias, so the over-trust replicates in all four and the fix works in two; a fifth, ORCA (an RVO2 port), keeps 0.88 with the bias always on and 0.60 with it yielding, so the fix works in three of five, and not only where the fitted bias is weak; with robots added to two of those crowds, robots that hold the opposite side cut the humans' keep-right share by 0.14 to 0.20 and lane order by 0.10 to 0.24 at 20% robots in both, robots that hold the crowd's side change neither, and the human delay per robot pass differs tenfold between the two models
summary: An open research programme on which passing policy a fleet of mobile robots should use in a corridor shared with people, with the crowd models fitted to real trajectories and cross-checked across model families (social force, ORCA, the anticipatory power law). Milestone 1 measures the human baseline in the Forschungszentrum Jülich HERMES bidirectional corridor experiments (2009; 24 runs; 4,752 walkers tracked at 16 fps; DOIs 10.34735/ped.2009.10–12). With no instruction about the exit, 1,016 of 1,084 walkers (0.937, two-stage bootstrap 0.865 to 0.993) walked on their own right, both streams on the same relative side, and lane order was 0.91 to 1.00 against 0.25 to 0.52 for shuffled directions. When each walker was told to leave by the left or right exit, the share fell to 0.534 (0.503 to 0.568) over 13 symmetric runs and 0.526 over the asymmetric set, and lanes persisted at lower order (0.59 to 0.85, above the null in every run). Three of five registered predictions held; the share did fall at the highest density (0.82) and the free-speed run walked at 1.73 m/s, above the predicted range. Milestone 2 replicates this on the independent BaSiGo corridor experiment (2013; 15 runs; 8,155 walkers; 4 m corridor; DOI 10.34735/ped.2013.5) with predictions registered first: with no exit instruction 0.924 (0.877 to 0.973) kept right, inside the HERMES interval; with exits assigned by wristband it fell to 0.689 (0.566 to 0.839; difference +0.235, 0.073 to 0.365), a smaller collapse than at HERMES, stepping down at the instruction rather than drifting with run order. In the last two runs, with the exit instruction kept and ‘screen information’ added (content not documented by the archive), 1,212 of 1,218 walkers (0.995) kept right. All six registered predictions held; lane order beat the null in all 15 runs. Milestone 7 checks the convention outside the lab with a head-on encounter measure on the ETH/Hotel (Zurich) and UCY Zara (Nicosia) pavement recordings, after projecting every track back onto its video frames to fix each frame’s handedness: walkers kept right in 0.654 (0.592 to 0.741; 723 encounters) of Zurich passes and 0.680 (0.565 to 0.797; 491) of Nicosia passes, though Cyprus drives on the left; the same measure reproduces the lab’s 0.935 and 0.526. The street convention is real but far weaker than the corridor’s, and two scenes per city cannot separate a city norm from scene layout. Limits: ‘right’ assumes the archive frame is right-handed with z up; neither experiment randomised run order, so the instruction effect is descriptive, and what the BaSiGo screens showed is unknown; laboratory crowd of students; no robots yet. Milestone 3 fits a social-force twin (JuPedSim 1.4.2, Helbing–Farkas–Vicsek parameters, plus one steering bias toward one’s own right when someone approaches head-on) on the nine free-choice runs. Without the bias it keeps 0.51 right; the fitted bias (β = 0.1) gives 0.89 to 0.97 and lane order within 0.10 in 7 of 9 runs, but only 3 of 9 runs fall inside their intervals and the twin cannot congest past about 1.5 walkers/m² (the densest real run reached 3.8). On the 14 assigned-exit runs it never saw it keeps 0.78 on the right where people kept 0.54 (HERMES 3.6 m, pooled), overstating every run: the twin over-trusts the convention. Geometry (corridor length, exit positions) is assumed, as the archive was unreachable this session. Milestone 4a tests that: moving the assigned walkers’ exits from a quarter width in to the walls lowers the held-out share to 0.68, still above people in 13 of 14 runs, and a second family, JuPedSim’s anticipation velocity model (Xu, Chraibi and Seyfried 2021, default parameters), fitted the same way (β = 0.35), forms near-perfect lanes, fails H3 (4 of 9 runs in interval, densities unreachable) and keeps 0.996 on the right under assigned exits. In both families a side bias fitted on free-choice runs survives the goals that made people drop it. Milestone 4b tests the rule rather than the model: a bias that switches off for a walker whose exit lies on its left (walkers without a lateral goal, the only ones in the fitted runs, are unaffected, so nothing is refitted) cuts the mean held-out share error from 0.210 to 0.079 for social force, from 0.353 to 0.118 for a third family, JuPedSim’s collision-free speed model (Tordeux, Chraibi and Seyfried 2016; β = 0.2), and from 0.395 to 0.260 for the anticipation model. Pooled HERMES held-out share: 0.610, 0.623 and 0.877 against people’s 0.541. The collision-free speed model with the yielding bias is the only pair that also gets the held-out lanes (12 of 14 within 0.10). The rule was chosen after the earlier failures were seen, and no rule reproduces the run-to-run spread. Milestone 4c adds a fourth family from another code base, the anticipatory power law of Karamouzas, Skinner and Guy (2014), implemented in numpy with Inria UMANS’s closed-form force and parameters (k = 1.5, τ0 = 3 s; checked against a finite-difference gradient). Fitted the same way (β = 0.35) it keeps 0.971 on the right under assigned exits with the bias always on and 0.698 with the yielding bias (mean error 0.393 → 0.153). The over-trust replicates in all four families; the yielding fix brings the share within 0.10 in the two fitted with β ≤ 0.2, not in the two fitted with β = 0.35 (a pattern seen after the run). The power law fails H3 too, so no family of four reproduces side, lanes and speed-density together, and H3 is refuted. A fifth family, ORCA (optimal reciprocal collision avoidance, ported from RVO2 with UMANS parameters), needs the strongest bias (β = 1.0) and fits the free runs worst, keeps 0.878 with the bias always on and 0.600 with the yielding bias (mean error 0.312 → 0.086, lanes within 0.10 in 11 of 14). So the over-trust replicates in all five families, the yielding fix works in three, and the registered test of the β-strength pattern refutes it. ORCA fails H3 as well. Robots (milestone 5a): in the collision-free speed and social-force crowds, at 5, 10 and 20% robots walking 0.9 m/s, robots that hold the opposite side cut the humans’ share on own right by 0.14 to 0.20 and lane order by 0.10 to 0.24 at 20%, lateral-goal robots about half that, and crowd-side or adaptive robots neither. The two models rank the four policies alike by these lane costs (Kendall τ 0.67 to 1.0) but not by human delay (τ −0.67 to 0): an opposite-side robot pass costs people 12 to 63 s in social force and at most 4.6 s in the collision-free speed model. The proposal’s 0.5 m close pass is near zero in both. Robots here are agents of the crowd model with a lane rule, not a robot planner.
